309.title: karma: Vivekananda's Karma Yoga lectures · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna…
309.hook: a flute plays in the forest, and the cows stop chewing and the rivers slow down
309.tomorrow: jnana: a seed with nothing inside
309.howItsDone: Krishna is almost always shown with his flute, and devotees sing the gopis' songs from the Bhagavata; in many traditions the flute is taught as a picture of the devotee, empty of ego so God can play through them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road closed the week: desire and anger, like fire covered by smoke. Did you catch one pull and name it? Today, a new week, and the bhakti road. Day three hundred nine.

Think of a song that stops you. You're in a store, or a car, and it comes on, and for three minutes you're not in the store anymore. You're somewhere else, and you'd follow that sound anywhere. Now picture a forest in autumn, near the river Yamuna. The cowherd boys are driving the cows out to graze, and one of them lifts a bamboo flute to his lips. In the village, the young women called the gopis hear it. And according to the Bhagavata, so does everything else.
screen: `A SONG THAT STOPS YOU.` → `AUTUMN, NEAR THE YAMUNA.` → `A BAMBOO FLUTE.`

segments.voice: This chapter of the Bhagavata Purana is called the song of the flute, and it's told almost entirely through the gopis, talking to each other about what the music does. The cows, they say, stop grazing, with grass still in their mouths, ears lifted, tears in their eyes. The calves stop drinking their mothers' milk. The deer come out of the woods and stand still. The birds settle on the branches and close their eyes, as if listening in meditation. Even the rivers, the gopis say, show their feeling: they swirl, and slow, and offer lotus flowers at his feet. And then the gopis say something surprising. They're jealous of the flute. What did this piece of bamboo do, they ask, to get to drink the nectar of his lips, so often, when we can't? Now here's what devotees have heard in that jealousy for centuries. The flute is a plain thing. A hollow stick. Nothing inside. And many teachers say that's exactly why Krishna plays it. It's empty, so the breath passes through it and becomes music. On the bhakti road, the dream isn't to become impressive. It's to become hollow enough to be played. This reading isn't in the verses themselves; it's what generations of devotees have drawn from them. But it's why the flute is everywhere in Krishna's images, on temple walls and calendars and dashboards. The whole forest stops to listen, and the one thing that gets to touch his lips is a plain, hollow stick.
screen: `THE SONG OF THE FLUTE.` · `COWS, DEER AND RIVERS STOP.` · `THE GOPIS ENVY A PIECE OF BAMBOO.` · `HOLLOW ENOUGH TO BE PLAYED.` · then, large: `HOLLOW ENOUGH TO BE PLAYED.`

segments.voice: Sit, and imagine you're a length of bamboo. Hollow, light, open at both ends. Breathe in, and feel the breath move through you without catching on anything. Breathe out, and let it go all the way. Whenever a thought snags, a worry, a plan, a sore spot, notice it, and let the breath move it through. You don't have to make music. Just stay open. If you pray, you can ask to be played. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. In the song of the flute, the only action is letting the breath through, and the whole forest listens.
Your line: hollow enough to be played. Today, stop and really listen to one piece of music, start to finish. Day three hundred nine.

310.title: karma: Vivekananda's Karma Yoga lectures · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna…
310.hook: a father asks his son to break open a seed, and asks what he sees inside
310.carry: too fine to see, too real to deny
310.tomorrow: karma: a ghost who needs work, and a dog's curly tail
310.howItsDone: The banyan seed teaching of the Chandogya Upanishad is taught in Vedanta classes, sometimes with an actual fruit broken open, and the banyan tree itself is honored in many Hindu villages and temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhakti road: the song of the flute, and the gopis jealous of bamboo, hollow enough to be played. Karma, bhakti, jnana: today we return to Shvetaketu and his father. Day three hundred ten.

Somewhere near you there's a very big tree. Maybe an oak, or a maple, or, if you're in India, a banyan, with roots dropping from its branches like ropes, wide enough to shade a whole village meeting. That tree came from a seed smaller than a grain of rice. That part is common knowledge. But what's actually inside the seed? A father in the Upanishads asks his son to do exactly that.
screen: `A VERY BIG TREE.` → `FROM A VERY SMALL SEED.` → `LOOK INSIDE.`

segments.voice: We're back in the sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, where Uddalaka is teaching his son Shvetaketu with things from around the house. Last week, it was salt in water. This time: bring me a fruit from that banyan tree. Here it is, sir. Break it open. It's broken. What do you see? Tiny seeds, sir. Break one of those. It's broken. What do you see there? Nothing at all, sir. And the father says: this finest essence, the one you can't see, from that very thing this great banyan tree stands. Believe it, my dear. Then the refrain you already know: that finest essence is the Self of all this. That is the real. Tat tvam asi. You are that, Shvetaketu. Here's what's clever about the lesson. When Shvetaketu says nothing, he isn't wrong. He really can't see anything. But the tree is standing right there. So the father isn't asking him to stop trusting his eyes. He's showing him the limit of his eyes. Some things are too fine to see and too real to deny. On the jnana road, knowledge doesn't mean collecting more facts. Shvetaketu already had twelve years of those. It means learning to recognize what can't be pointed at, the way you recognize the salt by its taste and the seed by the tree. And notice the father's gentleness: my dear, believe it. Knowledge here begins with trust, and then becomes seeing.
screen: `BREAK THE FRUIT. BREAK THE SEED.` · `NOTHING AT ALL, SIR.` · `FROM THAT, THE GREAT TREE STANDS.` · `TOO FINE TO SEE, TOO REAL TO DENY.` · then, large: `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Sit, and imagine holding a single seed in your palm. So small you could lose it. Now picture the whole tree that could come from it: trunk, branches, a thousand leaves moving in the wind. Breathe in: the seed. Breathe out: the tree. Then turn the picture gently toward yourself. What's the smallest, finest thing in you, too fine to see? Don't try to find it. Just rest with the question, the way Shvetaketu stared at the broken seed. If you pray, you can offer the question. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. On the jnana road today, the action is small: break the seed, look, and trust what you can't see.
Your line: too fine to see, too real to deny. Today, look at one big tree for a full minute, and think of its seed. Day three hundred ten.

311.title: karma: Vivekananda's Karma Yoga lectures · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna…
311.hook: a man gets a ghost who will do any job, but will kill him the moment it runs out of work
311.howItsDone: The Ramakrishna Mission, founded by Swami Vivekananda, runs schools, hospitals and disaster relief as spiritual practice, and its monks and volunteers are taught to see service as a privilege rather than charity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: a banyan seed, broken open, too fine to see, too real to deny, and from that, the great tree. Today, back on the karma road, with Vivekananda's lectures and a ghost story. Day three hundred eleven.
screen: `TOO FINE TO SEE, TOO REAL TO DENY.`

segments.voice: Swami Vivekananda, lecturing on karma yoga in the 1890s, tells a story that sounds like a folk tale. A man wants a ghost to do his bidding. A sage gives him a charm, and the ghost appears and says: I'll do anything you command. But the moment I have nothing to do, I'll kill you. The man thinks: perfect. Build me a palace. Done. Bring me money. Done. Clear this forest. Done. Every job, finished in minutes. And the man realizes, with rising panic, that he's running out of jobs.
screen: `A GHOST THAT DOES ANY JOB.` → `EVERY JOB, DONE IN MINUTES.` → `RUNNING OUT OF WORK.`

segments.voice: He runs back to the sage. The sage says: see that dog with the curly tail? Tell the ghost to straighten it. So the ghost grabs the tail and pulls it straight. Lets go. It curls right back. Straightens it. Lets go. Curls. The ghost is at it day after day, the story says, until it gives up and makes peace with the man. Then Vivekananda explains. The world, he says, is like that dog's curly tail. People have been trying to straighten it for a very long time. Every generation thinks it will finally fix things for good, and the tail curls back. So why work to help anyone at all? Here's his surprising answer, and it's the title of that lecture: we help ourselves, not the world. The world doesn't need us to save it. It will go on, with its ups and downs. But the one who serves is changed by serving. Vivekananda called the world a great moral gymnasium, a place where we build strength by working in it. So he says something that turns charity upside down. When you help someone, don't feel proud. Be grateful. They gave you the chance to practice. That's why karma yoga can work without discouragement. You're not failing if the tail curls back. You were never really in charge of the tail. You're in charge of the work, and of the heart you bring to it. This isn't giving up on the world. Vivekananda himself founded a mission that still runs hospitals and schools and disaster relief. It's working without needing to win.
screen: `STRAIGHTEN THE DOG'S TAIL.` · `IT CURLS RIGHT BACK.` · `WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD.` · `BE GRATEFUL TO THE ONE YOU HELP.` · then, large: `WORK WITHOUT NEEDING TO WIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one problem you keep trying to fix that keeps curling back. A mess that returns, a conflict that won't settle, a cause that never seems to move. Let yourself feel the tiredness of it. Breathe in, and let go of needing it fixed forever. Breathe out, and hold on to the work itself: the next small, good action. Then think of one person you've helped, and quietly thank them for the chance. If you pray, you can offer that thanks. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action. In Vivekananda's lecture, good work doesn't straighten the world's tail. It straightens the worker.
Your line: the world's curly tail. Today, help one person, and then thank them. Day three hundred eleven.

312.title: karma: Vivekananda's Karma Yoga lectures · bhakti: the Bhagavata Purana's Krishna…
312.hook: a full moon, a flute, a circle dance, and a God who disappears the moment anyone feels special
312.carry: set it down, and see who's beside you
312.howItsDone: The rasa lila is performed in dance and drama, especially in Vrindavan and in Manipuri and other classical dance, and Vaishnava devotees read the gopis' love as the highest model of devotion to God, not as a pattern for human behavior.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: Vivekananda's ghost, and the world's curly tail. We help ourselves, not the world. Did you thank someone you helped? Today, the bhakti road, and a night under a full moon. Day three hundred twelve.

An autumn night, the moon full over the Yamuna. Krishna plays his flute at the edge of the forest. In the village, the gopis hear it, and they drop everything. One leaves the milk on the stove. One leaves a meal half served. One is halfway through putting on her makeup, one eye done. They run to the forest. And the first thing Krishna says when they arrive is: why are you here? It's night. Go home to your families. That's your duty.
screen: `A FULL MOON AND A FLUTE.` → `THEY DROP EVERYTHING.` → `GO HOME, HE SAYS.`

segments.voice: This is the rasa lila, from the tenth part of the Bhagavata Purana, and some devotees call it the heart of the whole book. The gopis won't go. They say: we've left everything for you. Where would we go? So he stays, and walks and laughs with them in the moonlight. And then something happens in the gopis' hearts. Each begins to feel proud, the best of women, singled out. And in that moment, Krishna disappears. The gopis search the forest, asking the trees and the vines if they've seen him. They act out his stories to feel close to him. They sing a song of longing, known as the Gopi Gita. When their pride is gone and only longing remains, he appears again. Then comes the rasa dance itself: a great circle, and Krishna multiplies himself so that every gopi feels he is right beside her. Now, how to hear this. Devotees hear it as the love of souls for God, not an ordinary romance. The Bhagavata itself, right after the dance, has a king ask how such a story fits with dharma. The answer: this is God's play, not a pattern for people to imitate, and whoever hears it with faith gains devotion and is freed from lust. Two teachings stand out. Pride makes God vanish; longing brings him back. And God is fully present to each person, not divided among them. In the circle, everyone is closest.
screen: `WE'VE LEFT EVERYTHING FOR YOU.` · `PRIDE, AND HE VANISHES.` · `LONGING, AND HE RETURNS.` · `A CIRCLE, AND HE'S BESIDE EACH ONE.` · then, large: `IN THE CIRCLE, EVERYONE IS CLOSEST.`

segments.voice: Sit, and notice any small pride in you right now, nothing dramatic. I'm doing well at this. I'm better than I was. Let it be there, and set it down gently, the way you'd put down a bag. Then notice what's left underneath: a longing, maybe, for peace, for closeness, for something you can't name. Breathe with that longing. You don't have to fix it. If you pray, you can let the longing itself be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry, and the gopis' action was running toward the flute, and letting go of pride once they got there.
Your line: set it down, and see who's beside you. Today, when you feel a flash of pride, let go of it. Day three hundred twelve.

313.title: karma: Vivekananda's Karma Yoga lectures · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana:…
313.hook: an ancient text says the gods would rather you didn't find out who you are
313.carry: drop every label, and feel: I am
313.tomorrow: karma: the crane, the wife and the butcher
313.howItsDone: Aham brahmasmi is one of the four mahavakyas, the great sayings, traditionally associated with the four Vedas and taught to renunciants in some Advaita orders; students of Vedanta meditate on it, each school reading it in its own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bhakti road: the rasa night. Pride, and Krishna vanished; set it down, and see who's beside you when he returns. Karma, bhakti, jnana: today the jnana road, and three of its boldest words. Day three hundred thirteen.

A herd of cows. They give milk, they pull the cart, they are a family's living. Suppose one of them wanders off one day, free. For the owner, losing even one is a nuisance, and losing many is worse. Here's the strange part. An Upanishad says the gods see people that way. It's not pleasing to the gods, it says, that people should come to know this. Know what? Three words.
screen: `A HERD OF COWS.` → `ONE WANDERS OFF, FREE.` → `THE GODS WOULD RATHER YOU DIDN'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad tells it like a creation story. In the beginning, this world was Brahman, the ultimate reality. And it knew itself, saying: aham brahmasmi. I am Brahman. By knowing that, it became everything. Then the text says: whoever awakens to this, among the gods, among the sages, among people, becomes that. Even now, whoever knows I am Brahman becomes all this, and even the gods can't stop them, because that person has become the gods' own Self. But someone who worships a god thinking, he is one and I am another, the text says, doesn't know. And then comes the cow line: just as many cows serve a person, each person serves the gods, and losing even one cow is unpleasant. So the gods aren't pleased when people learn this. It's a startling, almost funny picture, and it's pointing at something serious: in the text, whoever knows this can't be held back, not even by the gods. Aham brahmasmi is one of the four great sayings, the mahavakyas, beside the tat tvam asi you met with the salt and the seed. Tat tvam asi is the teacher saying: you are that. Aham brahmasmi is the student finally saying it from the inside: I am. Different schools hear it differently. Advaita hears strict identity. Ramanuja's and Madhva's followers read the same line within their own views, where the soul stays distinct and devotion stays whole. On the jnana road, the line is less a claim to argue than a place to look from.
screen: `IN THE BEGINNING, BRAHMAN KNEW ITSELF.` · `WHOEVER KNOWS THIS BECOMES ALL.` · `THE GODS AREN'T PLEASED.` · `YOU ARE THAT, THEN: I AM.` · then, large: `AHAM BRAHMĀSMI.`

segments.voice: Sit, and say the word I, silently, once. Notice where it seems to come from. Not your name, not your job, not your story. Just the plain sense of I am, here, now. Breathe in, and rest in I am. Breathe out, and let every label fall away, just for this breath. If a label comes back, that's fine: notice it, and return to the simple sense of being. You don't have to believe anything. Just look. If you pray, you can rest in God as the ground of that I. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. On the jnana road the action is knowing, and in the Upanishad, whoever knows I am Brahman can't be held back, even by the gods.
Your line: drop every label, and feel: I am. Today, once, drop every label and just feel: I am. Day three hundred thirteen.

314.title: karma: Vivekananda's Karma Yoga lectures · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana:…
314.hook: inside the butcher's house, the last instruction sends the monk straight back home
314.carry: the duty at your own door
314.tomorrow: bhakti: Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, and the line he couldn't write
314.howItsDone: The story of the woman and the righteous butcher, the Vyadha Gita of the Mahabharata, is widely retold in Hindu homes and sermons, often through Vivekananda's version, to teach that one's own daily duties, done selflessly, are a spiritual path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the jnana road: drop every label, and feel: I am Brahman, and gods who'd rather we didn't find out. Today the karma road, and the rest of a story from Vivekananda. Day three hundred fourteen.

Day two hundred sixty-three left a story at a door. A proud young monk who burned a bird with a glare. A woman who made him wait because she was caring for her husband. And a butcher in the market who fed his old parents before he would teach. Vivekananda tells it in his lecture What Is Duty? But he barely steps inside the butcher's house. The Mahabharata does. And the butcher's last instruction is the one thing the monk never expected to hear. Today, we go inside that house.
screen: `A DOOR, A BIRD, A BUTCHER.` → `INSIDE THE BUTCHER'S HOUSE.` → `THE LAST INSTRUCTION.`

segments.voice: Vivekananda gives only one exchange from inside. The monk, amazed by what he's heard, asks: with knowledge like yours, why are you in a butcher's body, doing such ugly work? And the butcher answers, in Vivekananda's telling, that no duty is ugly and no duty is impure. The rest, Vivekananda says, is one of the highest flights of Vedanta, and the Mahabharata gives it in full: the Vyadha Gita, the song of the hunter. There the monk has a name, Kaushika, and the city is Mithila. The butcher says his trade came down to him in his family. He sells meat; he doesn't do the killing. Then he turns the monk's disgust around. Nobody lives without harm, he says. The farmer's plow kills creatures in the soil. A walk down a path crushes tiny lives. What a person can choose is the rest: telling the truth, holding back anger, giving, and caring for the people in their keeping. He brings Kaushika in to meet his parents, and calls them his gods. And then he says the thing the monk least wants to hear. You left your own old father and mother, without their blessing, to go and study. They have grieved for you, the text says, until their eyes failed. Go home, and look after them. That's your practice. So the teacher Kaushika traveled all that way to find sends him straight back to where he started. Karma, on this road, isn't a grand mission somewhere far away. It's the duty that was waiting at your own door the whole time.
screen: `NO DUTY IS UGLY, NO DUTY IS IMPURE.` · `NOBODY LIVES WITHOUT HARM.` · `HIS PARENTS ARE HIS GODS.` · `GO HOME TO YOUR OWN PARENTS.` · then, large: `THE DUTY AT YOUR OWN DOOR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let one person come to mind whose care is partly yours. A parent, a child, a brother or sister, a friend who's been alone too long. Not someone you'd like to help someday. Someone close, maybe someone you haven't called in a while. Breathe in, and see their face. Breathe out, and notice one small thing they might need from you this week: a call, a visit, a meal. You don't have to do it now. Just let it become clear. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action. In the Vyadha Gita, a butcher teaches that no honest duty is impure, and sends a wandering monk home to his parents.
Your line: the duty at your own door. Today, do one thing for someone close to home, before anything farther away. Day three hundred fourteen.

fork.setup: you're Kaushika. you traveled all the way to Mithila to learn from this butcher. he's taught you, and now he gives you one last instruction. what is it?

go back to the forest and meditate harder.
fork.reveal: go home. the parents he left have grieved for him, and caring for them is his practice. the teacher sends the seeker back to where he started.

original.note: Sanskrit: duty, what ought to be done, from kri, to do; the same root as karma.

trapdoor: what you thought: the butcher's story is only about a humble job.
what it means: no honest duty is impure, and the duty nearest you, like the parents you left, comes first.

what a scholar hears: in the Vyadha Gita (Mahabharata, Vana Parva) Dharmavyadha calls his parents his highest gods and ends by sending Kaushika home to his own; Vivekananda's 'no duty is ugly' exchange is in Karma Yoga ch. 4.

315.title: karma: Vivekananda's Karma Yoga lectures · bhakti: the Gita Govinda · jnana:…
315.hook: a poet can't bring himself to write one line about God, goes to bathe, and comes back to find it written
315.tomorrow: jnana: Ramana Maharshi, and the afternoon he lay down to die
315.howItsDone: The Gita Govinda's songs are sung in temple worship, including at the Jagannath temple in Puri, and are performed in Odissi and other classical dance; devotees hear the love of Radha and Krishna as the love between the soul and God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the karma road: inside the butcher's house, the duty at your own door: a wandering monk sent home to the parents he left. Today the bhakti road opens a new book, and the week looks back. Day three hundred fifteen.

Eastern India, centuries ago. A poet named Jayadeva is writing a long poem in Sanskrit about Krishna and Radha, the gopi Krishna loves. He reaches a scene where Krishna, having hurt Radha, pleads with her to forgive him, and the line that comes to Jayadeva is shocking. Krishna asks Radha to place her foot on his head. God, asking a cowherd girl to put her foot on him. Jayadeva can't write it. It feels like too much. So he puts down his pen and goes to the river to bathe.
screen: `A POET WRITING ABOUT RADHA.` → `A LINE TOO BOLD TO WRITE.` → `HE GOES TO BATHE.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Gita Govinda, the song of the cowherd, and the story people tell goes on. While Jayadeva is at the river, his wife, Padmavati, sees him come back, pick up the manuscript, write something, and leave again. Then Jayadeva walks in from the river, dripping, and finds the line already written: the one he couldn't bring himself to write. He asks Padmavati who wrote it. You did, she says. You came back a few minutes ago. And he understands, the story says, that Krishna himself came and finished the line. That's a legend, not history. But look at what it's saying. The Gita Govinda tells of spring in the forest, of Krishna wandering among the gopis, of Radha hurt and jealous and hiding, of a friend carrying messages between them, of Krishna's longing and apology, and finally their reunion. It reads like a love poem, and it is one. Devotees hear it as the soul and God: the soul's hurt, God's longing, and a love so real that God would bow to the one who loves him. That's the heart of the line Jayadeva couldn't write. On the bhakti road, God isn't only the one we bow to. Sometimes God bows. Now look back at our week on three roads. On the bhakti road: the flute, the rasa night, and today the poem. On the jnana road: the banyan seed, and I am Brahman. On the karma road: the ghost and the curly tail, and the woman and the butcher.
screen: `THE GITA GOVINDA: SONG OF THE COWHERD.` · `THE LINE WRITTEN WHILE HE BATHED.` · `HURT, LONGING, REUNION.` · `SOMETIMES GOD BOWS.` · then, large: `DEHI PADA-PALLAVAM UDĀRAM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of a time someone you'd hurt forgave you, or a time you forgave someone. Let the memory be there, without replaying the whole argument. Feel the moment where the distance closed. Breathe in, and feel what it's like to be taken back. Breathe out, and feel what it's like to take someone back. Those two feelings are the whole poem. If you pray, you can rest in God's longing for you. The bell holds the time.
Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. In the Gita Govinda, the boldest action belongs to God: bowing to the one he loves.
Your line: sometimes God bows. Today, be the first to apologize for one small thing. Day three hundred fifteen.

original.note: Sanskrit: gita, song + govinda, the cowherd, a name of Krishna. Jayadeva's poem.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gita Govinda is another name for the Bhagavad Gita.

what a scholar hears: Jayadeva's poem is built of songs called ashtapadis, of eight verses each, and was sung in the Jagannath temple at Puri.
